transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lena (Redwood SE), Mark (Redwood Solutions), Priya (Orion ML Infra), Daniel (Orion VP Eng), Aisha (Orion SRE), Tom (Orion ML Eng)

Summary (auto): Technical deep dive on GPU runtime profiling focusing on kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA graphs stability, KV cache behavior and batching/quantization impact. Action items and follow-ups captured.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — we got Priya, Daniel, Aisha, Tom from Orion; Lena and Mark and myself from Redwood. Is that right?
[00:08] Priya: Yep that's right, thanks for setting this up. We're mainly looking for a deep dive on runtime perf — kernel selection, how TensorRT-LLM compares to vLLM for our workloads, and whether CUDA graphs actually help at our seq lengths. Also VPC/on-prem notes.
[00:20] Samir: Perfect. Lena's going to lead the profiling notes and run through results we've seen and gaps to test with you.
[00:28] Lena: Cool, I'll start with an overview. Quick disclaimer: some names in the slides may be off — transcription etc — but the numbers are from our internal runs. We profiled a couple of models: a 13B transformer and a 70B LLM variant, both FP16 and also 4-bit quantized runs. For engines we compared Redwood's TensorRT-LLM path (our TRT integration + kernel selector), and a vLLM-based path on CUDA with our batching and KV cache.
[00:55] Daniel: When you say kernel selector, what exactly are you picking between? cuBLAS/GEMM kernels vs fused attention?
[01:03] Lena: Right. Kernel selection here means choosing between vendor-provided fused attention + flash attention kernels, Triton-based custom kernels, and cuBLAS/cuDNN GEMM/convolution fallbacks. TRT-LLM tends to prefer CUDA graph-friendly fused kernels and TensorRT optimized layer implementations, while vLLM paths often use more generic flash attention or Triton custom kernels with different memory patterns.
[01:28] Aisha: We've seen warmup costs blow our p95; curious about CUDA graphs — do they reduce tail for short lived sessions?
[01:35] Lena: Good question. In our tests, CUDA graphs reduce dispatch overhead and stabilize p50->p95 for steady-state streaming workloads, but they can be brittle on dynamic sequence lengths. For batched, consistent seq lengths, CUDA graphs gave us 10-18% latency reduction and 12-20% throughput uplift depending on batch shape. For dynamic, you need either a graph per shape or a fallback to regular kernels which increases complexity.
[02:00] Tom: Do you prebuild graphs for every prompt length? That's infeasible for us because we have lots of interactive prompts.
[02:06] Lena: We typically build graphs for common lengths — e.g., 32, 64, 128 — and route other lengths to a fallback runtime. Also prefix/KV caching reduces repeated work for long contexts. But yes, if you're fully interactive with arbitrary lengths, the benefit is smaller unless you can bucket lengths.
[02:22] Priya: Tell us more about KV cache behavior across TRT vs vLLM. Does one have a clear advantage for memory and latency?
[02:29] Lena: vLLM has a more flexible KV cache architecture — it's designed to keep key/value shards on GPU memory with careful caching and spill to host. Our TRT path uses a different KV layout optimized for TensorRT's execution model; it can be more memory efficient at inference time because fused kernels reduce intermediate allocations, but it can be less flexible for streaming appends. In practice, for long-context streaming, vLLM's cache is slightly more robust; for short bursts with high throughput, TRT-LLM wins on per-token latency.
[02:58] Daniel: Any numbers to share?
[03:00] Lena: For a 13B model at batch size 8, seq=128 steady-state: TRT-LLM 90-110ms p50 per token, vLLM path 110-140ms p50 per token. Throughput wise TRT showed ~15% higher tokens/sec in that setup. For 70B quantized runs at batch 1, TRT-LLM FP16 gave lower latency p50 but vLLM with quantization-friendly kernels had better memory utilization, letting us fit larger context. Those are approximate and workload-sensitive.
[03:30] Aisha: What about quantization? We want int4/4-bit for cost but worried about degenerations and kernel availability.
[03:36] Lena: Quantization tradeoffs: INT8/4-bit ops need specialized kernels. TRT-LLM benefits from TensorRT's quantization pipelines and fused kernels that are heavily optimized; vLLM has community kernels and Triton-backed paths that are improving quickly. We observed that TRT's int8 pipelines gave consistent latency wins but sometimes required calibration steps that add offline cost. For int4 there's still fragmentation — some kernels are experimental and brittle. Our recommendation: start with 8-bit quantization plus mixed precision, run quality evals on your prompt set; then try 4-bit in a controlled POC.
[04:10] Tom: On a POC, can Redwood run both paths in parallel for apples-to-apples?
[04:15] Samir: Yes, we can replicate your prompt set across both runtimes. That's one of the trial offers — we can instrument and provide per-token latency traces and kernel selection logs. We'll share the benchmarking spreadsheet.
[04:23] Priya: Great. A few infrastructure Qs: for on-prem/VPC, how stable are CUDA graphs across driver versions and multi-tenant hosts? We've had graph replay failures when the driver stack changed.
[04:33] Lena: That's a known issue. CUDA graphs depend on ABI/driver stability. In our Private deployments we recommend pinned driver and CUDA runtime versions and a controlled rollout when you update drivers. Multi-tenant noisy neighbors can affect memory placement and lead to graph replay failures. We have a fallback mechanism to recompile graphs at runtime, but that introduces jitter. For regulated environments we usually recommend reserved capacity (dedicated GPUs) with pinned drivers.
[04:58] Daniel: What about preemption on shared clusters — if your graph is invalidated, do you restart the graph or fall back to non-graph kernels?
[05:05] Lena: We fall back to non-graph kernels and optionally recompile the graph asynchronously. The fallback increases latency for a short period but keeps service available. This is why dedicated pools with reserved capacity reduce those incidents.
[05:15] Aisha: Can the KV cache be sharded across multiple GPUs for big context?
[05:20] Lena: Yes — we support kernel-level KV sharding and model parallel splits. There are two common patterns: (1) KV sharding across GPUs where each GPU holds a slice of the KV memory, and (2) offloading cold segments to host or NVMe. Sharding reduces per-GPU memory pressure but increases all-reduce/collective costs on attention in some models. Our profiling tool shows the tradeoff and recommends a split for your model/config.
[05:44] Tom: You mentioned profiling tools — what artifacts do you provide?
[05:47] Mark: We provide per-token latency traces, kernel timeline traces (with approximate kernel names), CUDA graph build logs, memory allocation traces, and a benchmark spreadsheet that correlates prompt shapes with p50/p95. We'll also attach raw nvprof/nvtx-like traces where possible.
[06:00] Priya: Helpful. Any surprises we should expect when migrating from a CPU or less optimized setup?
[06:05] Lena: Typical surprises: (a) batch shapes matter a ton — you might get much better throughput with micro-batching strategies; (b) prefix caching can reduce token costs dramatically for chat-style workloads; (c) quantization can expose corner cases in generation quality — need eval harness; (d) CUDA graphs are great but need operational discipline on drivers and shapes.
[06:25] Daniel: On batching — our app is interactive, p99 matters more than throughput. How do you recommend balancing batching vs low latency?
[06:31] Lena: For interactive apps we use small batching (1-4) with tail-aware policies: we let requests wait a small window (e.g., 5-10ms) to accumulate a micro-batch for much better throughput without impacting p99 significantly. Also adaptive batching that looks at request inter-arrival distributions helps. We can tune on your traces.
[06:50] Priya: Anything about kernel selection logs we should know? Sometimes vendor kernel names are opaque.
[06:55] Lena: True — kernel names can be cryptic. Our logs map kernel invocations to higher-level operators and annotate whether they were TensorRT fused kernels, Triton kernels, or cuBLAS fallbacks. We also mark why a kernel was chosen (e.g., unsupported seq len for fused path).
[07:10] Tom: For our POC, we'd like to test: 1) TRT-LLM FP16 vs vLLM FP16; 2) 8-bit quantized runs on both; 3) CUDA graphs for common lengths; and 4) KV cache behavior under a streaming workload.
[07:20] Samir: Sounds good. We'll set up tests mirroring that. Quick question about data retention and privacy for logs — Priya?
[07:27] Priya: We need logs anonymized and stored in our VPC if possible. Also KMS integration for keys.
[07:32] Samir: We can provide S3 logs to your VPC endpoint or share via secure transfer; KMS/HSM options available for Private deployments. We'll include SOC2 docs in the follow-up packet.
[07:40] Aisha: One more performance edge case — what about attention cache reuse across multiple similar prompts? Any caching at higher levels?
[07:47] Lena: We support prefix caching and reuse when the prefix matches exactly. For near-duplicate prompts we have a heuristics layer that can hash prefixes and reuse cached KV if similarity is exact; fuzzy reuse is risky because of tokenization differences. We're experimenting with approximate matching but it's not production-ready.
[08:05] Daniel: Any recommended driver/CUDA combos you prefer? We run on internal infra with A100/80GB.
[08:10] Lena: For A100-80GB we recommend CUDA 12.x with matching NVIDIA driver that's tested with your TensorRT and cuBLAS versions. We maintain a compatibility matrix. For TensorRT-LLM, TensorRT 9.x with CUDA 12.x gave the most stable fused kernels in our tests. We'll share exact versions in the docs.
[08:27] Priya: Cool. Can we get a short sample command to run a CUDA graph build locally so our infra team can try?
[08:32] Lena: Yes, we'll add the smoke-test commands to the benchmark doc — simple script that builds graph for seq 32/64 and runs a couple of iterations while collecting nvtx markers. I'll put that in the next steps.
[08:42] Tom: Anything else about model compilation times? For CI we need to know how long graph compilation or TRT engine build will take for a 70B quantized model.
[08:49] Lena: TRT engine builds for 70B can take from tens of minutes to a few hours depending on optimizations and calibration steps. CUDA graphs compile faster — seconds to minutes per shape — but combined tuning (fused kernels + TRT engine) is heavier. We'll estimate based on your model and share ranges.
[09:05] Priya: Let's recap next steps.
[09:08] Samir: Recap: (1) Share benchmark spreadsheet and raw logs (Samir). (2) Provision trial dedicated capacity (Samir/ops). (3) Lena to send CUDA graph smoke-test commands and run initial tests with Tom. (4) Priya confirm VPC/on-prem/KMS requirements. (5) Redwood to send SOC2 and driver compatibility matrix.
[09:25] Daniel: Great, thanks. When can we get the trial provisioned?
[09:28] Samir: We'll aim to provision in 48-72 hours once you accept the trial NDA; I'll send details today.
[09:34] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:37] Samir: Thanks all.

End of call.
